title: Momentum and Impulse
seo_title: Physics 1: Momentum and Impulse Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
standard_text: Momentum and impulse; the conservation of momentum; elastic and inelastic collisions; springs and elastic energy. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, Physics 1, Quarter 2)
meta_desc: Free Physics 1 worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Quarter 2): work and energy, springs and elastic energy, momentum and impulse, collisions and momentum problems. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Momentum is conserved in every collision; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.
body_html:
How to think about it

The work–energy theorem: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy. A spring obeys Hooke's law F = kx and stores elastic energy Ee = ½kx².

Momentum p = mv is a vector. Impulse FΔt equals the change in momentum, so a longer stopping time means a smaller force (air bags, helmets). With no external force, total momentum is conserved. In an elastic collision kinetic energy is also conserved; in an inelastic collision some becomes heat and sound.

Example

A spring (k = 200 N/m) is stretched 0.10 m. Elastic energy?

E = ½ × 200 × 0.10²

Answer: 1.0 J

Example

A 2.0 kg cart at 3.0 m/s hits and sticks to a 1.0 kg cart at rest. Final speed?

6.0 kg·m/s = 3.0 kg × v

Answer: 2.0 m/s

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting that momentum has a direction (signs for opposite motions).
  • Assuming kinetic energy is conserved when objects stick together.
  • Using x instead of x² in elastic potential energy.

faq.q: Why does an air bag reduce injury?
faq.a: It makes the stopping time longer, so the force needed to stop the person is smaller.

faq.q: What is a perfectly inelastic collision?
faq.a: A collision in which the objects stick together and move as one.
